verses.context: Jacob summons all his sons for the words he will speak before he dies. He frames what follows not as a will but as a disclosure of the future, "what will happen to you in the days to come".
verses.grammar: He'asefu, "Gather around", is a Niphal imperative of asaf, to gather. The same verb closes the chapter twice: Jacob is ‘about to be gathered’ to his people (v. 29), and at the end he ‘gathered his feet’ into the bed and ‘was gathered’ to his people (v. 33). The poem is framed by the sons gathered to hear and the father gathered to his fathers. Yiqra ("will happen") is a by-form of qarah, to meet or befall. The phrase be'acharit hayyamim is discussed in the chapter note.

verses.context: The summons is repeated as the first couplet of the poem. Its two lines set the pattern of the whole: parallel lines that say one thing twice, the second sharpening the first.
verses.grammar: The couplet is in synonymous parallelism: hiqqavetsu veshim'u benei ya'aqov, ‘assemble and listen, sons of Jacob’, is matched by veshim'u el-yisra'el avikhem, ‘and listen to Israel your father’. Jacob and Israel, the two names of one man, stand in parallel. Qavats ("come together") is a close synonym of asaf in verse 1; the prophets use it for God regathering scattered Israel (Isaiah 43:5, Ezekiel 11:17).

verses.context: Reuben's saying opens with everything the firstborn should have been: his father's strength, the first sign of his vigor, preeminent in dignity and power. The praise sets up the reversal of verse 4.
verses.grammar: Reshit oni, "the beginning of my strength", is the same phrase Deuteronomy 21:17 uses to define a firstborn's right: "the firstfruits of his father's strength". Yeter se'et veyeter az, ‘excess of dignity and excess of power’, uses yeter, surplus or preeminence, twice. The next verse turns the same root into a verb, al-totar, "you will no longer excel": the one who had yeter will not yatar.

verses.context: The reason for Reuben's loss: he slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine (35:22). Jacob heard of it at the time and said nothing (35:22); here, decades later, he speaks.
verses.grammar: Pachaz kammayim, "Uncontrolled as the waters", uses pachaz, reckless or wanton; the related participle describes Abimelech's "reckless men" in Judges 9:4. Water boiling over is the image: strength without restraint. The last line changes person abruptly, from "you went up to your father's bed" to ‘he went up to my couch’ (alah, third person). Many readers hear Jacob turning away in disgust, speaking of Reuben rather than to him. Chillalta, "defiled", is the Piel of chalal, to profane, a word for treating the holy as common.
verses.history: Reuben's tribe settled east of the Jordan (Numbers 32) and never produced a judge, king, or prophet. Deborah's song rebukes Reuben for staying by the sheepfolds while others fought (Judges 5:15-16), Dathan and Abiram, leaders of the rebellion against Moses, were Reubenites (Numbers 16:1), and Moses' blessing prays only that Reuben may survive: "Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few" (Deuteronomy 33:6).

theology.note: A single act, long unmentioned, is not forgotten. The verse shows judgment working through the natural consequence of unrestrained character: the man who could not govern himself does not govern his brothers.

verses.context: Simeon and Levi are paired, not as brothers by birth only but as partners in the massacre at Shechem (34:25-31). Jacob names their weapons for what they were.
verses.grammar: Shim'on velevi achim, "Simeon and Levi are brothers", uses achim with a pointed sense: brothers in the deed. The same two are called "Dinah's brothers" when they take their swords to Shechem (34:25). Kelei chamas, "weapons of violence", uses chamas, the word for the violence that filled the earth before the flood (6:11, 13). Mekherotehem, translated "their swords", occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain; ‘swords’ is a contextual guess, and others suggest ‘plans’ or ‘schemes’.

verses.context: Jacob dissociates himself from their deeds. He will not be part of their council, because they killed in anger and maimed animals at will.
verses.grammar: Two negative wishes stand in parallel: be-sodam al-tavo nafshi, ‘into their council may my soul not come’, and biqhalam al-techad kevodi, ‘with their assembly may my glory not be joined’. Sod is an intimate circle of counsel; qahal an assembly. Kevodi, ‘my glory’, stands in parallel to nafshi, ‘my soul’, as in Psalm 16:9 and 57:8, where it means one's inmost self; some scholars repoint it as kevedi, ‘my liver’, a Hebrew image for the inner person. Ish ("men") and shor ("oxen") are singular nouns used collectively. Iqqeru, "hamstring", is the Piel of aqar, to cut the leg tendons, as Joshua did to the Canaanite horses (Joshua 11:6).
verses.text: Genesis 34:28 says Simeon and Levi's party took the Shechemites' flocks and herds, not that they maimed them. Some interpreters take verse 6 as describing an incident not narrated there; others take the line as poetic intensification of the same wanton violence. A few ancient readers vocalized shor as shur, ‘wall’, reading ‘they tore down a wall’.

verses.context: Jacob curses their anger, not the men, and announces that they will be scattered among the tribes. The judgment falls on both, but it will be worked out very differently in each tribe's history.
verses.grammar: Arur appam, "Cursed be their anger", is a passive participle placed first. The object of the curse is the anger and wrath, not Simeon and Levi themselves, a precise distinction. The two reasons are introduced by ki: their anger az ("strong", ‘fierce’) and their wrath qashatah ("cruel", literally ‘hard’). The last pair of verbs is first person, achalleqem and afitsem, ‘I will divide them’ and ‘I will scatter them’: Jacob speaks as the one through whom the verdict comes.
verses.history: Simeon's allotment lay within Judah's territory (Joshua 19:1, 9), and the tribe largely merged into Judah; Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 does not mention Simeon at all. Levi received no territory but forty-eight towns scattered through all the tribes (Numbers 35:1-8, Joshua 21), because the LORD himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20). Their loyalty at the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29) turned the scattering into a priestly calling.

theology.note: The same sentence of scattering becomes loss for Simeon and blessing for Levi. God's judgment in Scripture is real, but it is not a fate that closes off his mercy; what a later generation does with the sentence matters.

verses.context: Judah's saying begins. After three sons rebuked, the fourth is promised praise, victory over enemies, and the homage of his brothers. The rule of the family passes to Judah.
verses.grammar: Yehudah attah yodukha achekha, "Judah, your brothers shall praise you", is a pun: yodukha (from yadah, to praise, Hiphil) plays on the name Yehudah, which Leah gave with the words "This time I will praise the LORD" (29:35). "Your father's sons shall bow down to you" (yishtachavu lekha) repeats the blessing Isaac gave Jacob, "may the sons of your mother bow down to you" (27:29), and recalls Joseph's dreams of his brothers bowing (37:7-10). The honor Joseph dreamed of in his youth is here given in its royal form to Judah.

verses.context: Judah is pictured as a lion: young and returning from the kill, then at rest in a strength no one dares to disturb. The image is of settled, secure power.
verses.grammar: Gur aryeh, "a young lion", is literally ‘a lion's cub’. Mitteref beni alita, ‘from the prey, my son, you have gone up’, uses teref, prey torn by a beast; the verb from the same root was Jacob's cry over Joseph's robe, tarof toraf yosef, "Joseph has surely been torn to pieces" (37:33). The son who once helped deceive his father with that robe is now the lion rising from its prey in another sense. The last lines, kara ravats ke'aryeh ukhelavi mi yeqimennu, "he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?", are quoted almost exactly by Balaam of Israel (Numbers 24:9). Lavi may mean lioness or simply lion; the parallel pair is common in Hebrew poetry.

nt.note: John hears the risen Christ announced as "the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David", the one worthy to open the scroll. The title takes this verse's lion and joins it to Isaiah 11:1, 10 (the root of Jesse). John then turns and sees not a lion but a Lamb standing as though slain (Revelation 5:6): the ruler from Judah conquers by sacrifice.

verses.context: The heart of Judah's saying. Royal authority will remain with Judah until a climactic arrival, when the obedience of the peoples belongs to the ruler from Judah. The chapter note's hard question sets out the readings of ‘Shiloh’.
verses.grammar: Lo-yasur shevet, "The scepter will not depart", pairs shevet (scepter) with mechoqeq, a Piel participle of chaqaq, to inscribe or decree. It can mean ‘the one who decrees’ (the KJV's ‘lawgiver’) or, in parallel with scepter, the commander's staff, which a seated ruler held upright ‘between his feet’. Ad ki ("until") marks a point of arrival, not necessarily the end of the rule: the scepter stays until it reaches its goal. Yiqqehat, "allegiance", is rare, found elsewhere only in Proverbs 30:17 (‘obedience’ to a mother); it means submission, the obedience of peoples, ammim, a word that reaches beyond Israel.
verses.text: The consonants read in most manuscripts as shiloh can also be divided as shello, ‘which belongs to him’, and many medieval Hebrew manuscripts spell it shloh, which supports that reading. The Septuagint renders the phrase as ‘until the things stored up for him come’, the Syriac and Targum Onkelos as ‘until he comes to whom it belongs’, Onkelos adding that this is the Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs. A commentary on Genesis from Qumran (4Q252) reads the verse as looking to the coming of the righteous Messiah, the branch of David. Ezekiel 21:27 appears to echo the ‘to whom it belongs’ reading.

theology.note: The verse gives Judah a scepter that lasts until a climactic ruler arrives whom the nations obey. Ancient Jewish readers took that ruler as the Messiah; Christians see the royal line pass through David to Jesus (Hebrews 7:14), whose reign draws the obedience of the nations (Romans 1:5).

Kingship in Israel is first promised in a family blessing, long before Israel has a king. The rule of God's people is set within God's promise from the start, not invented later as a political convenience.

verses.context: The ruler's time is pictured as overflowing plenty. Vines are so abundant that a donkey can be tied to the best of them, and wine so plentiful that clothes can be washed in it.
verses.grammar: Oseri ("He ties") and beni atono (‘his donkey's son’, "his colt") both carry an old ending in -i on the first word of a construct phrase, a feature of archaic Hebrew poetry, one reason scholars count this among the Bible's oldest poems. Ir ("donkey") and ben-atono (‘son of his she-donkey’) are the same pair of words Zechariah uses for the king who comes "humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9). Dam-anavim, "the blood of grapes", is a fixed poetic phrase for wine (Deuteronomy 32:14).

theology.note: The ruler's reign brings an abundance that reverses the curse on the ground (3:17-19). The prophets use the same picture of overflowing wine for the age of restoration (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18).

verses.context: The final lines of Judah's saying describe the ruler himself as a picture of health and abundance: eyes darkened with wine, teeth white with milk.
verses.grammar: The two comparisons can be read in two ways. The preposition min can mark comparison, "darker than wine" and "whiter than milk" (BSB, NIV), or cause, ‘dark from wine’ and ‘white from milk’. Chakhlili, "dark", is rare; the related noun describes the "redness" or dullness of the drunkard's eyes in Proverbs 23:29. On the first reading the verse praises beauty; on the second it continues verse 11's picture of a land so rich its people are sated with wine and milk.

verses.context: Zebulun, Leah's sixth son, comes before Issachar, her fifth, a reversal of birth order that Moses' blessing keeps (Deuteronomy 33:18). Zebulun's saying is about geography: the sea, ships, and the northern coast toward Sidon.
verses.grammar: The line repeats chof, ‘shore’ or ‘coast’: lechof yammim yishkon vehu lechof oniyyot, ‘to the shore of seas he will dwell, and he to a shore of ships’. Yarkhato, "his border", is literally ‘his flank’ or ‘thigh’ (yarekh), the far side of his territory, reaching toward Sidon.
verses.history: Sidon was the leading Phoenician port on the coast of modern Lebanon, and in Genesis the firstborn of Canaan (10:15). Zebulun's allotment in Galilee (Joshua 19:10-16) does not appear to touch the sea, so the saying is usually taken to describe the tribe's access to coastal trade routes, as Deuteronomy 33:19 speaks of Zebulun feasting on "the abundance of the seas". Isaiah 9:1 names Zebulun and Naphtali by "the Way of the Sea", the words Matthew applies to Jesus' ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:13-16).

verses.context: Issachar is a strong donkey resting between the folds, who likes his good land so much that he accepts forced labor to keep it. Comfort is bought with freedom.
verses.grammar: Chamor garem, "a strong donkey", is literally ‘a donkey of bone’, big-boned and sturdy. The word translated "sheepfolds", mishpetayim, is a dual of uncertain meaning (it recurs in Judges 5:16): ‘sheepfolds’, ‘saddlebags’, or ‘hearths’ have all been proposed. The key phrase is lemas oved, "submitted to labor as a servant", literally ‘became forced labor, working’. Mas is the technical word for the corvée, the forced labor Solomon imposed (1 Kings 9:21) and Israel imposed on Canaanites (Joshua 16:10). Menuchah ("resting place") is the word later used for the rest God gives in the land (Deuteronomy 12:9).
verses.history: Issachar's territory lay in the fertile Jezreel Valley (Joshua 19:17-23), the most productive farmland in the north and a corridor for armies and trade. Scholars have compared this saying with an Amarna letter (EA 365) in which Biridiya, ruler of Megiddo in the fourteenth century BC, reports supplying corvée workers to cultivate fields at Shunem, a town later in Issachar's territory.

verses.context: The sons of the maids begin with Dan, Bilhah's firstborn. Small as the tribe will be, Dan will act as one of the tribes of Israel, securing justice for his own people.
verses.grammar: Dan yadin ammo, "Dan shall provide justice for his people", is a pun on the name: the verb din, to judge or vindicate, is the root of Dan. Rachel named him with the same verb, "God has vindicated me" (30:6, dananni). Ke'achad shivtei yisra'el, "as one of the tribes of Israel", uses shevet in its sense of tribe, the word that meant ‘scepter’ in verse 10.

verses.context: Dan's second image is a small snake by the road that brings down a horse and rider. The small tribe will win by ambush, not by numbers.
verses.grammar: Nachash, "snake", is the word for the serpent of Genesis 3, and shefifon ("viper") occurs only here; it is usually identified as a horned viper that lies hidden in sand. Hannoshekh iqqevei-sus, "that bites the horse's heels", uses aqev, heel, the word of 3:15 and the root of Jacob's own name (25:26). The verb vayyippol ("tumbles") is a narrative form after participles, describing the result as a completed event.
verses.history: Dan failed to hold its first allotment on the coastal plain (Judges 1:34) and migrated to the far north, where it took the town of Laish by surprise and renamed it Dan (Judges 18:27-29). Samson, the Danite judge, fought the Philistines alone and by cunning rather than with an army (Judges 13 to 16).

verses.context: In the middle of the sayings, Jacob breaks off to pray. The line stands alone, addressed not to his sons but to the LORD, and it is the only use of the divine name in the poem.
verses.grammar: Lishu'atkha kivviti YHWH, ‘for your salvation I wait, O LORD’. The object, ‘your salvation’, is placed first for emphasis. Kivviti is a Piel perfect of qavah, to wait with expectation; the noun tiqvah, hope, comes from the same root. The perfect describes a waiting that has been going on and continues, not a single moment. The chapter note discusses yeshu'ah.

theology.note: Jacob's only prayer in the poem is for the LORD's deliverance, placed amid predictions of his sons' wars and struggles. The tribes' future rests on the LORD's salvation, not on their lion strength or their cunning.

Prayer here interrupts prophecy. Rashi connected the line with Samson, the Danite of verse 17, who at the end cried to God for strength (Judges 16:28); read more broadly, the line is the dying father's own confession that he waits for God to act.

verses.context: Gad's saying is a single line of sound play: raided by raiders, he will raid back at their heels. The tribe on the eastern frontier will be attacked but will answer.
verses.grammar: Gad gedud yegudennu vehu yagud aqev: four words built on the sound g-d. Gedud is a raiding band, and gud the verb to raid or attack. The saying plays on Gad's name, though at his birth Leah linked it with good fortune (30:11).
verses.text: The Hebrew reads aqev, ‘heel’, and begins verse 20 with me'asher, ‘from Asher’. Many scholars and translations move the letter m from the start of verse 20 to the end of verse 19, giving aqevam, ‘their heels’, and leaving verse 20 to begin simply ‘Asher’. The BSB follows that division ("their heels" and "Asher's food").
verses.history: Gad settled east of the Jordan (Numbers 32), exposed to raids from Ammon, Moab, and the desert. The Moabite Stone of King Mesha, from the ninth century BC, mentions that ‘the men of Gad’ had long lived in the land of Ataroth. Chronicles praises Gadite warriors whose faces were like the faces of lions (1 Chronicles 12:8).

verses.context: Asher's land will be rich, producing food fit for kings. The saying is a pure blessing of fertility.
verses.grammar: Shemenah lachmo, "food will be rich", uses shamen, fat or rich, the word for fertile land (Numbers 13:20). Ma'adannei-melekh, "royal delicacies", are dainties fit for a king. The name Asher means happy or blessed (30:13, "How happy I am"), and the saying fits the name.
verses.history: Asher's territory ran along the fertile coastal plain and western Galilee north of Mount Carmel (Joshua 19:24-31), olive country, which Moses' blessing celebrates when it prays that Asher may "dip his foot in oil" (Deuteronomy 33:24).

verses.context: Naphtali is a doe running free. The second line is read in two very different ways by English Bibles.
verses.text: The Hebrew vowels read hannoten imrei-shafer, ‘who gives beautiful words’. The BSB's "that bears beautiful fawns" repoints imrei (‘words of’) as immerei, ‘lambs of’ or ‘young of’, keeping the animal image of the first line. The KJV and NASB keep the traditional reading (‘he gives goodly words’), and some connect it with the Song of Deborah and Barak, since Barak was from Naphtali (Judges 4:6, 5:1).
verses.grammar: Ayyalah sheluchah, "a doe set free", uses a Qal passive participle of shalach, to send or let go: a hind let loose, swift and unconfined. The image may describe the tribe's freedom in the hill country of upper Galilee.

verses.context: Joseph's saying, the longest after Judah's, begins with an image of fruitfulness, probably playing on the name Ephraim (41:52, "God has made me fruitful"). The fruitful son of Rachel is pictured flourishing by a spring.
verses.grammar: Ben porat yosef is literally ‘a son of a fruitful one is Joseph’. Porat is a feminine participle of parah, to be fruitful, the root of Ephraim's name. The next line is difficult: banot tsa'adah alei-shur, ‘daughters, she climbs over a wall’, mixes a plural subject with a singular verb. "Branches" (BSB) takes banot, ‘daughters’, as offshoots of the vine. Other scholars read porat as related to pere, wild donkey, and translate ‘Joseph is a wild colt ... wild asses on the hillside’, a reading adopted by the Jewish Publication Society's 1985 translation.

theology.note: The saying opens by naming Joseph's life as fruitful, the word Joseph himself gave his second son in Egypt (41:52). What his brothers meant as an end became a spring-fed vine.

verses.context: Joseph was attacked by archers who hated him, but his bow held steady, because the Mighty One of Jacob strengthened his arms. The saying reads Joseph's whole story as attack survived by God's strength.
verses.grammar: Vayyistemuhu, "aimed at him in hostility", is from satam, to bear a grudge or hate persistently. It is the verb for Esau's grudge against Jacob (27:41) and for the brothers' fear after Jacob's death, "What if Joseph bears a grudge?" (50:15). Ba'alei chitsim, ‘masters of arrows’, are the archers. Be'eitan ("steadied", ‘in firmness’) describes a bow that did not waver. Avir ya'aqov, "the Mighty One of Jacob", appears here for the first time; Isaiah takes it up (Isaiah 49:26, 60:16), and Psalm 132:2 uses it. The Hebrew of the next line reads mishsham ro'eh even yisra'el, ‘from there, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel’; the BSB's "in the name of" follows a small change of vowels (mishshem, ‘from the name’), a reading found in some ancient versions.

theology.note: Jacob gathers names for God in a single line: the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd (compare 48:15), and the Stone or Rock of Israel. Each names God by what he has been to Jacob: strength, care, and a sure foundation, possibly with a memory of the stone at Bethel (28:18-22).

verses.context: The blessing of Joseph widens: from the God of his father, who helps him, and from the Almighty, blessings from the sky, from the deep below, and from breast and womb. It covers rain, groundwater, and fertility.
verses.grammar: Birkhot, "blessings", is repeated three times in this verse and twice more in verse 26. The phrase "the depths below" is tehom rovetset tachat, ‘the deep crouching beneath’: tehom is the deep of 1:2 and 7:11, and ravats, to crouch or lie, is the verb of Judah's lion (v. 9) and of sin crouching at the door (4:7). Shaddai, "the Almighty", is echoed in shadayim, "breasts", a sound play that ties the name to the gift of fertility.
verses.text: The traditional Hebrew reads ve'et shaddai, ‘and with Shaddai’. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read ve'el shaddai, ‘and God Almighty’, matching the title in 48:3. The BSB's "by the Almighty" fits either reading.

theology.note: The blessing names the whole created order, heaven above, the deep below, and the body's power to bear and nurse, and puts all of it in the hand of the God of Jacob. Fertility is God's gift, not the domain of the fertility gods of Canaan.

verses.context: Jacob's blessings surpass even the enduring blessings of the ancient hills, and he asks that they rest on Joseph's head, the one set apart from his brothers. Moses' blessing repeats the closing line almost word for word (Deuteronomy 33:16).
verses.grammar: Nezir echav, "the prince of his brothers", uses nazir, one set apart or consecrated, the word that also names the Nazirite (Numbers 6:2). Joseph was set apart from his brothers first by their hatred and then by his elevation. Qodqod, ‘crown of the head’ (BSB "brow"), parallels rosh, ‘head’.
verses.text: The traditional Hebrew reads horai, ‘my progenitors’, giving ‘the blessings of your father have surpassed the blessings of my progenitors’. The BSB's "ancient mountains" follows a different division of the consonants, harerei-ad, ‘everlasting mountains’, supported by the Septuagint and by the parallel in Deuteronomy 33:15 ("the ancient mountains" and "the everlasting hills") and Habakkuk 3:6. The second reading gives a neater parallel; the first says that Jacob's blessings exceed those of Abraham and Isaac.

verses.context: Benjamin, the youngest, is a ravenous wolf, devouring prey in the morning and dividing plunder in the evening. The last saying is not of the protected child of chapters 42 to 44 but of a fierce warrior tribe.
verses.grammar: Ze'ev yitraf, "a ravenous wolf", is literally ‘a wolf, he tears’, using the same verb as Judah's ‘prey’ (teref, v. 9). Babboqer yokhal ad velaerev yechalleq shalal, ‘in the morning he eats prey and at evening he divides spoil’: morning and evening together describe unbroken success. Chalaq ("divides") is the verb used of Simeon and Levi's scattering (v. 7).
verses.history: Benjamin produced fierce fighters: Ehud the left-handed judge (Judges 3:15), the seven hundred left-handed slingers (Judges 20:16), and Saul, Israel's first king (1 Samuel 9:1-2). The tribe nearly destroyed itself in the civil war of Judges 19 to 21. The apostle Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1, Philippians 3:5), and several early Christian writers, among them Tertullian, read the wolf who seizes prey in the morning and shares the spoil in the evening as a figure of Paul, first persecutor and then apostle.

verses.context: The narrator closes the poem: these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said. Everything he said, including the rebukes, is called a blessing, each son receiving what fitted him.
verses.grammar: Shivtei yisra'el shenem asar, "the tribes of Israel, twelve in all", is the first time the Bible names the twelve tribes as such. The sons have become tribes in the narrator's own words. The final clause repeats the root barakh three times: vayvarekh otam ish asher kevirkhato berakh otam, ‘he blessed them, each according to his blessing he blessed them’.

theology.note: Twelve individuals become the twelve tribes in this verse. Jesus' choice of twelve apostles, who will judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28), and the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem named for them (Revelation 21:12) look back to this moment.

verses.context: Jacob's last instructions repeat to all his sons the charge he gave Joseph under oath (47:29-31): bury me with my fathers in the cave of Machpelah. He describes the site in legal detail, as if reading from the deed of chapter 23.
verses.grammar: Ani ne'esaf el-ammi, "I am about to be gathered to my people", is a Niphal participle of imminent action. Being gathered to one's people is distinct from being buried: Jacob is ‘gathered’ at his death in Egypt (v. 33), but buried in Canaan weeks later (50:13). The description piles up relative clauses (asher, ‘which’, three times) and names the field, the cave, Mamre, Canaan, the seller, and the purpose, la'achuzzat-qaver, "as a burial site", the legal language of 23:17-20.
verses.history: Machpelah lay east of Mamre, at Hebron (23:19). The traditional site is enclosed by a massive stone wall built in the time of Herod the Great, in the first century BC, and it has been a place of Jewish, Christian, and Muslim pilgrimage for centuries.

theology.note: Jacob's last words are about a grave in the land of promise. Owning nothing in Canaan but this cave, he insists on lying there, a claim on the future that only God's promise can make good.

verses.context: Jacob lists who lies in the cave: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. It is the only place Genesis reports where Rebekah and Leah were buried, and Jacob, who loved Rachel more, chooses to lie beside Leah.
verses.grammar: Three times Jacob says shammah qaveru, ‘there they buried’, and the third time shifts to the first person, shammah qavarti et-le'ah, "there I buried Leah". The rhythm places Jacob's own act last. Verse 32 begins miqneh hassadeh, ‘the purchase of the field’: miqneh here means an acquisition by purchase (from qanah, to buy, as in 23:18), not ‘livestock’, its more common sense.
verses.history: Genesis narrates the burials of Sarah (23:19), Abraham (25:9-10), and Isaac (35:29) but not those of Rebekah or Leah. Rachel, who died on the road, lies near Bethlehem (35:19, 48:7). Leah, the unloved wife (29:31), shares the family tomb with the patriarchs and with Jacob.

verses.context: Jacob finishes his charge, draws his feet into the bed, breathes his last, and is gathered to his people. The death of the last patriarch is told in one sentence.
verses.grammar: The verb asaf appears twice: vayye'esof raglav el-hammittah, ‘he gathered his feet into the bed’, and vayye'asef el-ammav, "he was gathered to his people". The first is Jacob's own act, the second the passive (Niphal) of the same verb, describing what happens to him. Vayyigva, "breathed his last", is the verb used at the deaths of Abraham (25:8), Ishmael (25:17), and Isaac (35:29). The text does not use the ordinary verb for dying (mut) here, a detail on which the Talmud (Ta'anit 5b) built the saying that ‘Jacob our father did not die’, though 50:15 later speaks of his death plainly.

theology.note: Being gathered to one's people happens at death, before and apart from burial, which suggests that the patriarchs understood death as joining those who had gone before rather than simple extinction. Jesus cites God as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to show that the dead live to God (Matthew 22:32).
